meta.title: Swahili — Sounds and spelling
meta.subtitle: 41 sounds and rules of agreement — start here, beside Swahili A1
meta.desc: How Swahili is read, and how its words agree, before or beside the first word: 41 notes, one card each — 26 sounds (the five vowels, the doubled vowel, the stress, and the 19 consonant spellings an English reader says wrongly: ch, sh, ny, ng', ng, g, j, r, the Arabic dh, th, gh and kh, the m and n that are a syllable of their own, and mb, nd, nj, nz, mv) and 15 rules: that Swahili has no tones, the noun classes, what a noun's class does to an adjective, to “of”, to this and that and to the numbers that agree, the people and animals that take m-wa agreement whatever their class, is and is not (ni, si), the verb's subject prefix, to have (kuwa na), the tense markers, the negative, the short verbs that keep ku-, the commands, and the Swahili clock. Swahili is spelled as it sounds, so the sounds are few; what they hold is what the spelling does not tell an English reader. Of Swahili A1's 522 one-word headwords, 20 begin with an m or an n that is a syllable (mtu, nchi), 28 have the ng of finger, 11 ny, 21 ch, 25 sh, 9 an Arabic dh, th, gh or kh, 41 a j and 28 a doubled vowel. AND THE AGREEMENT, which every sentence uses: a Swahili noun belongs to a class, and the adjective, the possessive, “of”, this and that and the verb each take a prefix chosen by it. The level decks show the forms — 192 cards of Swahili A1 carry a plural, 40 a row of agreeing forms for the five pairs of classes, 118 a verb's present, negative and commands — and the rule cards here say what the pattern in those rows is, each with a table of forms read off A1's own cards. The front shows the spelling or the question. The back gives the sound in the International Phonetic Alphabet and the English sound the key compares it to, the key's own example, then the first words of the Swahili A1 deck that have it, with a speaker beside each, the letters picked out, and the word's own transcription from the dictionary where it has one (ˈ stands before the stressed syllable, a dot between syllables). Say the word, then press the speaker and compare. THE ORDER is the vowels, the stress, the consonants, then the rules. At the default of ten new cards a day the deck takes 5 days; it is meant to be studied beside Swahili A1, not finished first. — WHAT IS NOT HERE: nothing is written for this deck. Each sound, each example and each English comparison is a cell of the sound's row in the key named first below, and each sentence a sentence of one of the four pages, a paragraph of its own, with a cut marked […]. The letters that sound as an English reader expects (b, d, f, h, k, l, n, p, s, t, v, w, y, z) have no card. No sentence was found to quote for two things a learner is usually told, so neither has a card: that two vowels side by side are two syllables (kuamka, chai), and that the days are numbered from Saturday (Jumamosi, the first; Jumapili, the second). The rule cards show only forms an A1 card shows, so the past, future and perfect are the tails the dictionary prints (-lisoma, -tasoma, -mesoma), to go behind a subject prefix. The speaker is your device's Swahili voice reading the example word, so a device without one is silent. — Sounds, examples and English comparisons: Wikipedia, “Help:IPA/Swahili”, revision 1265646459 of 2024-12-27. Rules: Wikipedia, “Swahili”, revision 1387179866 of 2026-11-22; Wikipedia, “Swahili grammar”, revision 1387011184 of 2026-11-22; Wikipedia, “Date and time notation in Africa”, revision 1339899124 of 2026-02-22 (all CC BY-SA 4.0). Transcriptions: English Wiktionary, via kaikki.org (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example words, forms and meanings: the Swahili A1 deck on this shelf (English Wiktionary via kaikki.org, CC BY-SA 4.0).

fields.Letters: What a noun's class does to an adjective: -zuri
fields.Says: The class of the noun determines the forms of other parts of speech that relate to it, such as verbs, adjectives, etc. This process is called agreement or concord.Inflecting adjectives are words which describe a noun or pronoun and take the following prefixes, which are very similar to the prefixes found on nouns.

fields.Letters: A person or an animal outside the m-wa class: rafiki, baba
fields.Says: Swahili phrases agree with nouns in a system of concord but, if the noun refers to a human, they accord with noun classes 1–2 regardless of their noun class.Animate nouns (referring to a person or animal) are an exception and these occur with concords of the noun classes 1 (singular) or 2 (plural).

fields.Says: The genitive preposition -a (sometimes termed a "connector", "possessive" or "associative" preposition) has a similar role to that of the genitive case of some other languages. It indicates the possessor, or a more general association, and roughly corresponds in meaning to the English preposition "of". It receives a prefix that agrees with the preceding noun's class.

fields.Says: The demonstratives in Swahili may be used either as adjectives, with a noun, or as pronouns, standing alone. They occur in three types:Proximal ("this, these"), referring to something near the speaker.Medial/Referential ("the aforementioned"), referring to something that has been previously mentioned.

fields.Letters: is and is not: ni, si
fields.Says: The invariable copula ni is used, in the present tense, to express that two noun phrases (the subject and complement) refer to one and the same referent:The negative form si can be used in all the same situations with a negative meaning:Because ni and si do not provide any information about the subject, personal pronouns, usually only necessary for emphasis, frequently appear.
fields.Examples:

si/si/negative present (all persons, numbers, and classes) of -wa (“to not be”)

fields.Letters: Who does it: the prefix on the verb
fields.Says: Both the subject and, when applicable, the object of the verb are indicated by prefixes or concords attached to the verb stem. Swahili is a pro-drop language: explicit personal pronouns are only used for emphasis, or with verb forms that do not indicate subject or object.The negative subject concords are formed by prefixing the syllable ha- to the beginning, except for the irregular forms si- (instead of *hani-), hu- (instead of *hau-) and ha- (instead of *haa-) which are used, respectively, for first, second and third person singular animate subjects.

sisi (we)tunahatuna
ninyi (you)mnahamna

fields.Examples:
the cards

fields.Says: There is no dedicated verb meaning 'to have'. Its equivalent is kuwa na, literally 'to be with', using the comitative preposition na. In the present tense, however, kuwa na has special contractions, whereby the subject prefix is attached directly onto -na. Note that kuwa na has an existential meaning when the subject is in a locative class.
fields.Pairs:

fields.Examples:
the cards
kuwa nato have

fields.Says: Prefixes are always attached in a fixed order; the object prefix always comes last, immediately before the verb stem, while the subject prefix comes before the object prefix.The past tense is used in Swahili to talk about actions or states in the past, whether in the near or the distant past. It is formed with the prefix -li-.The future tense is formed in Swahili with the prefix -ta-.The perfect is formed in the positive with the prefix -me-.
fields.Examples:
the cards
kusomato read
kutakato want
kufanyato do
kuonato see, to find

fields.Says: The final -a is replaced with another vowel in certain grammatical contexts, becoming -i in the present negative, and -e in the subjunctive and imperative forms involving an object prefix.What these verbs share in common is that they are all loan-words and none of them end in -a. The consequence of this is that they do not take the suffixes -e and -i that the verbs ending in -a do

fields.Letters: The short verbs: kula, kunywa, kuja, kwenda
fields.Says: Short verbs are those which, in their infinitive form, consist of only two syllables, such as kula "to eat", kunywa "to drink", kuja "to come", kupa "to give".The positive tense marker -li- cannot take stress and triggers the use of the extension -ku- (or -kw-) where necessary.

fields.Says: This difference arises because Swahili timekeeping begins at sunrise rather than midnight. The first hour of daylight (7:00 a.m. in the Western system) is saa moja (hour one). Therefore, 8:00 a.m. is the second hour, or saa mbili. This effectively creates a 6-hour offset between the Swahili and Western methods of counting time.
